item.title: Running the Quarterly Security Audit for the First Time: What Actually Broke
item.dc:creator: Ronald G. Thomas
item.description:
WarningDraft

This post is a work in progress and may change.

A control verified once is a control verified once. Nothing about that guarantees it is still true today.

Introduction

The series hub recommends a quarterly audit: a fixed checklist, run against every machine, that re-verifies controls instead of assuming they still hold. This post reports the first full run of that audit across the fleet, in the last week of September 2026, and the week of follow-up work it triggered. The audit was planned as an afternoon. It took several days, rebuilt one machine from bare metal, gave the home server a second job, and produced a list of findings in which none of the original threat model’s controls failed. Full-disk encryption was on everywhere. The password store and its key were intact. The failures were in the spaces between controls.

Note

Part 8 of the security series; start with Security Foundations for a Multi-Machine Research Fleet for the overview.

The findings are told in the order they surfaced, each as a short account of what was checked, what broke, how it was found, and what changed. The lasting practice behind each one is described in depth in the post that owns the topic, and each finding links there.

Motivations

  • A security posture configured once and never re-checked degrades quietly. The only way to know whether it still holds is to look.
  • The fleet had grown to five machines (three Macs, a Linux laptop, and a Linux home server), and the Linux machines had never been held to the same standard as the Macs.
  • Several categories of risk, notably OAuth grants and backup coverage, had no row in the original threat model, and the audit was the first time either produced a live problem.
  • Backups that report success are not the same as backups that cover what they should. The audit was the first systematic comparison of the two.

Objectives

  1. Run the hub’s audit checklist against all five machines and record every deviation.
  2. Bring the Linux laptop to parity with the Macs: disk encryption, keys, password store, dotfiles, and its own backup.
  3. Compare what each backup job actually covers with what it was meant to cover, by reading logs and exit statuses rather than schedules.
  4. Turn every finding into a fix, verified on every machine it touches, and a line in the fleet’s written reference.

What is a quarterly audit?

The audit is a checklist, not an investigation. The canonical copy lives in the series hub; in outline it asks, for every machine: is the disk encrypted; which keys exist and where are they authorized; where do secrets live, and does anything sync or print them; which scheduled jobs exist, are they loaded, what was their last exit status, and what do their logs say; and does every repository and backup destination point where it should. The point of a fixed list is that it is run the same way each quarter, so a deviation stands out rather than being explained away.

What the first run showed is that most failures are not found by the check that targets them. They are found by a neighboring check, or by doing ordinary work carefully: reading a log line that should not be there, noticing a modified file in a repository nobody touched, or running a fix on the second machine and watching it fail.

Prerequisites

This post assumes the fleet and controls described in the earlier parts of the series:

  • the five machines and the threat model (part 1);
  • pass with GPG for credentials (part 2) and on-demand loading of other secrets (part 3);
  • dotfiles in a git repository instead of a synced folder (part 4);
  • Borg, cloud copies, and Time Machine (part 5);
  • the home server, mercury (part 6).

No code needs to be run to follow it. The few commands shown are the checks actually used.

The Findings

1. Credentials with the wrong coverage

Checked: where every secret on every machine lives, and whether that location is backed up, synced, or both.

Broke: coverage was wrong in both directions. Two machines held their Borg passphrases only in a plain file on the machine being backed up, not in the password store. Losing either machine would have meant losing the ability to decrypt its own backup on the home server. At the same time, the files holding API keys and cloud credentials (.Renviron, .env, the AWS credentials folder) were in no backup at all, with no other copy anywhere.

Found by: walking the home folder of each machine and comparing it with each backup job’s include list, item by item.

Changed: every Borg passphrase now lives in pass, confirmed to match the copy in use. The secret-holding files were added to every machine’s Borg include list, and a backup was run and verified on each. The rules for where secrets may live are in part 3.

2. The exposure, and what rotation actually involved

Checked: whether any secret had ever been somewhere it should not.

Broke: a personal settings folder on two Macs had for months been a symlink into a synced cloud folder. Everything saved there, including the GPG private key, both machines’ backup passphrases, the cloud-storage OAuth tokens, and an API key, had been syncing to the provider’s servers. Older leftover copies of the password store sat there too.

Found by: following the symlink. Nothing about daily use revealed it.

Changed: because access by anyone else could not be ruled out, every exposed credential was treated as compromised and replaced: a new GPG key with the store re-encrypted to it, new Borg passphrases, new SSH keys for both code hosts, new rclone OAuth tokens, a new gh token, and a new app password. The step that mattered most came after revoking: testing that each old credential was actually dead. Most were. A Copilot token and an old GitLab key were still live and had to be revoked separately. The migration away from the synced folder, and how to delete a shared copy safely, are in part 4; rotation discipline is in part 3.

3. One revocation, every machine logged out

Checked: each machine’s login state for the tools that hold OAuth tokens.

Broke: during the audit two tokens were exposed by the audit itself. A routine “which account is this connected to” check on one tool printed a complete, live token to the terminal, and inspecting a plaintext token file on another machine did the same. Both were revoked at once, as a printed secret is a rotated secret. Each revocation logged out every machine using that client, not only the one being fixed, because an OAuth grant belongs to the pairing of account and client application, not to one machine’s session.

Found by: the next morning’s failures on machines nobody had touched.

Changed: before revoking any grant, the list of machines that will need to log in again is written down first. One machine’s gh token had also been stored in a plain file rather than the Keychain; it was reissued into the Keychain like the others. Part 3 covers the practice.

4. A login token inside the dotfiles repository

Checked: git status in the dotfiles repository on a machine where nothing had been changed.

Broke: a modified file appeared that nobody had edited. The gh tool’s configuration folder is one of the folders under ~/.config that the dotfiles setup symlinks into the repository, so every gh auth login on any machine had written that machine’s live login token into a file inside the repository’s working tree. It had happened on every machine. By luck it had never been committed: the only version in the history was the blank template from when the repository was created. It was a loaded gap rather than a past leak, one careless git commit -a away from putting a live token into the repository’s history.

Found by: the unexpected modified file.

Changed: that file is now excluded from the repository on every machine, so gh keeps working with its file in the usual place while git no longer tracks it. The broader lesson is that a rule which symlinks whole configuration folders will eventually carry a credential nobody meant to share. Secret scanning on commit is the recommended guard (part 3).

5. The Linux laptop, from bare metal

Checked: the Linux laptop, zeus, against the same list as the Macs.

Broke: nearly everything, in the sense that it had never been configured: no disk encryption, no shared credential access, no backup.

Changed: zeus was reinstalled with LUKS full-disk encryption (unlike FileVault, it must be chosen before partitioning), given its own keys, the GPG key copied over a trusted channel and verified to decrypt before being trusted, the password store and dotfiles cloned, and a nightly Borg backup scheduled as a systemd user timer. Two Linux differences mattered. The backup script looked for its tool in the Mac package manager’s locations, which a one-line per-machine override file fixed without forking the script. And a user timer on Linux keeps running after logout only if lingering is enabled for the user; without it, the backup would have looked configured and stopped the first time the session ended. The whole process is now a written runbook rather than memory.

6. Backup coverage that vanished with a folder

Checked: what each Borg archive contains, against what it was meant to contain.

Broke: the include lists on the three Macs named the project, documents, and utilities folders indirectly, through the old synced folder they used to be symlinked into. When that folder was removed, Borg began skipping all three, logging a one-line warning each night and otherwise reporting success.

Found by: reading one morning’s backup log line by line.

Changed: the lists now name the folders directly. File counts per archive went from about 24,000 to between 68,000 and 88,000 per machine, which confirmed the missing content was now captured. Borg does not fail when a listed path disappears, by design, so coverage has to be checked by reading the log (part 5).

7. Two machines racing for one cloud destination

Checked: the destinations of the nightly cloud copies.

Broke: julia and athena each mirrored their own copy of the project folder to the same cloud location. A mirror treats the other machine’s version as drift to be corrected, so whichever ran last won, and neither copy was reliably complete. The same jobs had also never excluded regenerable caches; one night’s upload ran fifteen hours on tens of thousands of tiny files.

Changed: every machine now has its own destination folder, and the jobs exclude the same regenerable categories Borg already skips (part 5).

8. A self-referencing link that stopped every deletion

Checked: each cloud job’s log, not its schedule.

Broke: every run on both machines ended in errors. A student repository contained a link pointing to itself. The cloud copies follow links (rclone sync -L), hit the loop, and, as a safety measure, skipped every deletion for the run. Files deleted or renamed locally were never removed from any cloud copy, which kept growing, while each run looked routine.

Changed: the link was removed on every machine that had it, and the cloud copies now run cleanly. Watching for listing errors in these logs is part of the backup check (part 5).

9. Skipped runs that looked like failures, and the fix that broke joe

Checked: why one machine’s cloud copy had not run for three nights.

Broke: each job takes a lock so two runs to one destination cannot overlap. When the lock was held by a long manual run, the scheduled job gave up with exit status 1 and logged nothing, indistinguishable from a real failure.

Changed: a skipped run now logs a dated line and exits with its own code:

/opt/homebrew/bin/flock -n -E 75 "$lock" \
  rclone sync -L "$PRJ_ROOT" "$dest" "$@" || rc=$?

That fix then broke joe. It calls the lock tool at a fixed path, and joe had never installed it, so every cloud job there failed at once. Installing it revealed that joe had never had rclone configured either: its cloud jobs had been scheduled for weeks with nothing able to run. They were removed, since Borg covers joe. The fix had been tested on one machine and rolled out to three.

10. An address the router chose

Checked: a general status check of the Macs’ scheduled jobs, a few days after the audit.

Broke: the home server had been restarted for routine work and the home router gave it new addresses. athena and joe still reached it by the old one, so their nightly Borg backups timed out and failed for three nights, while each scheduler recorded the failure the whole time. The first fix changed the address in the general SSH configuration and the backups still failed: the Borg script deliberately uses its own SSH configuration file, so that only the restricted backup key is offered, and the address lived there too. A day later, a check that also covered the Linux machines found that zeus had been failing the same way for four nights. The first status check had looked only at the Macs.

Changed: every Borg client now reaches the home server by its Tailscale address, which does not change, as julia already did. The new address was trusted only after confirming the server’s host key matched the one recorded for the old address. The networking practice is in part 6; the backup side is in part 5.

The checks themselves were one line per platform:

# macOS: last exit status of each backup agent
launchctl list | grep -E 'borg|rclone'
# Linux: result of the last Borg run
systemctl --user show -p Result,ExecMainStatus borg-backup.service

11. A job that left the scheduler

Broke: julia’s Borg job had dropped out of launchd, apparently at a restart, with its definition file intact, so a night passed with no run at all. A job that is not loaded produces no failure to notice.

Changed: the job was loaded again and a manual run verified. The status check now confirms that jobs are loaded, not only that their last run succeeded. A related hazard surfaced the next night: a Mac’s 02:00 job can fire during a brief dark wake before the network is up and fail, so a backup script should wait or retry for connectivity before giving up (part 5).

12. Archives that never expired

Checked: how much space the Borg repositories used, and why.

Broke: nothing had ever pruned an archive. Every repository grew without limit.

Changed: a retention policy (two weeks of dailies, two months of weeklies, a year of monthlies, three years of yearlies) is now applied by hand each quarter. Automating it would require each repository’s passphrase on the machine that stores it, which is exactly what the design prevents: the storage host can append but cannot decrypt. The manual step is the design working, not a gap in it (part 5).

13. A second service and no firewall

Changed situation: athena’s Time Machine drive moved to the home server and was shared over Samba, giving a single-purpose machine a second job.

Broke: the server had no firewall running. Its security had rested on the narrow restricted backup keys and on nothing else listening. That was an implicit assumption, never a decision, and it stopped holding when a second service appeared.

Changed: ufw now denies incoming connections by default, trusts the Tailscale interface, and allows SSH and Samba only from the home network (part 6).

14. Time Machine: a file system that could not be checked, and a missed checkbox

Broke, twice. The external drive was first formatted HFS+, chosen deliberately because both macOS and Linux can read it. Within a week the drive dropped off USB in the middle of a write, and the Linux HFS+ checker could not verify the volume afterward. A backup volume that cannot be checked on the machine it is attached to is not one to trust, so it was reformatted ext4, a documented choice for this setup. Separately, the first Time Machine backup to the share was created without encryption, which Time Machine offers only when a destination is first added. It had reached 258 GB of one Mac’s files, unencrypted, on another machine before the omission was noticed.

Changed: the unencrypted backup was deleted, the freed space trimmed, and the backup restarted with encryption on and its password stored in pass. The setup is described in part 6 and the policy in part 5.

15. A share that listened only to itself

Broke: after the server restart in finding 10, Samba was configured to listen on one named Wi-Fi adapter, started before that adapter had an address, and listened only on the server’s loopback address. The share was unreachable from the network and nothing reported an error. The server also turned out to have two adapters on the same network, with Samba bound to only one, so connecting by name reached the refused address about half the time.

Found by: a direct write test on the server succeeded while athena could not connect; checking what Samba was actually listening on explained why.

Changed: Samba now waits for the network at boot and listens on both adapters. It is tested from another machine after a restart, not only on the server itself (part 6).

16. Making a full backup affordable

Checked: why athena’s Time Machine configuration excluded applications and system libraries.

Changed: rather than excluding them, the installed applications on all three Macs were cut back to a research minimum. A cleanup script removed each application’s support files while refusing to touch anything carrying the identifier of an application being kept, which mattered: one office suite’s uninstall list would otherwise have taken a kept word processor’s data with it. The full TeX distribution was replaced with per-user TinyTeX and a package list in the dotfiles repository, and the remaining applications are recorded in a Brewfile. With a small application set, Time Machine backs up everything except data that is regenerable or held elsewhere, and a reinstall has a list to work from.

17. One login for git

Checked: how each repository authenticates to the code host.

Broke: nothing, yet, but the mix was a liability: most project repositories used SSH keys while the dotfiles repository used the gh tool’s login.

Changed: project repositories moved to HTTPS remotes authenticated through the gh credential helper, whose token sits in the Keychain. A script rewrote only remotes pointing at the code host (over a hundred on the primary workstation) and confirmed along the way that no confidential, local-only repository had acquired such a remote. Two consequences were worth knowing in advance: the token needs the workflow scope before it can push changes to automated workflow files, and a command run over a plain SSH session into a Mac cannot reach the Keychain login, even though scheduled jobs in the logged-in session can. The same pass caught a blog post folder still pointing at the template repository it was copied from; it now has its own.

18. A host added later, and a firewall that was off

Changed situation: the Linux laptop became a second host for offloaded simulations: an always-on role, with sleep disabled and the lid closed, reachable from the whole home network.

Checked: its firewall, for the first time. The audit of this machine in finding 5 used the same list as the Macs, and that list had no firewall item.

Broke: the firewall was installed but inactive, so SSH was open on every network interface, Wi-Fi included. As with finding 13, nothing had decided this: it was simply how a machine that had never been a server arrived.

Changed: the same default-deny policy as the home server: incoming connections denied by default, everything trusted on the Tailscale interface, SSH allowed only from the home network. Afterward each way in was checked to still work (a login over the home network, a login over Tailscale, the simulation service, and the local-network name), because a firewall that locks the owner out is also a failure. The Macs’ firewalls were not part of this work: one was seen to be on, with stealth mode; the other two were not checked.

Things to Watch Out For

  • Revoking an OAuth grant logs out every machine using that client. List the machines that will need to log in again before revoking.
  • Some tools print raw secrets on an ordinary status check. Know which ones, and treat anything printed as exposed.
  • Symlinking whole configuration folders into a repository sweeps in files nobody chose, including login tokens. Check git status on machines where nothing changed.
  • Borg does not fail when an included path disappears. Read the log, and check file counts after any folder move.
  • Two machines mirroring to one destination race; they do not back each other up. Give each machine its own destination.
  • One self-referencing link can make rclone skip every deletion, while the run still looks routine.
  • A skipped run and a failed run should not share an exit status.
  • An address assigned by the router is not an identity. Reach always-on machines by a stable address, and know every file that names them; a restricted key’s separate SSH configuration is easy to forget.
  • A job that is not loaded produces no failure. Check that scheduled jobs are loaded, not only that they last succeeded.
  • Options that can only be chosen at setup, such as Time Machine encryption, will eventually be missed at setup. Verify the result immediately.
  • A service bound to a named interface can start before the interface exists. Make it wait for the network, and test from another machine after restarts.
  • A single-purpose machine’s security is often implicit. When it gains a second purpose, check what actually filters incoming connections.

What Did We Learn?

Lessons Learned

  • Verify by reading logs and exit statuses, not by trusting schedules. Every backup failure in this post was already recorded by the scheduler or in a log. None was announced. A job that is scheduled, a job that ran, and a job that covered what it should are three different claims.
  • A fix is not done until it has run on every machine it touches. The lock fix was correct and broke joe. The address fix was correct on two machines and missed the third. The status check that found the outage covered the Macs and missed the Linux laptop.
  • The blast radius of a fix is not always one machine. OAuth revocations, shared scripts, and broad symlink rules act on everything that uses the same mechanism. Know which kind of fix is in hand before applying it.
  • Rebuilding a machine from bare metal is the cheapest audit available, because a fresh machine has no accumulated exceptions hiding real gaps.
  • Write it down. Every finding went into the fleet’s internal reference the day it was fixed, which is why the second week’s failures were diagnosed in minutes rather than hours.
  • A machine’s role can change after its audit, and the audit does not follow. The laptop passed the list as a workstation; becoming a server added exposure the list never asked about, twice (findings 13 and 18). Re-run the relevant checks whenever a machine gains a job.

Limitations

  • The audit checked the architecture this series describes. It was not a penetration test and does not claim to have found every gap.
  • Several findings came from incidents observed directly, not from a systematic check, so there is no guarantee every instance of those problems has been found.
  • The reinstall runbook has been exercised on one machine.
  • Every failure here was found by a person looking. Until an automated check exists, the backups are only as verified as the last time someone read their status.

Opportunities for Improvement

  1. A daily status check that reports, for every machine including the Linux ones, each backup job’s loaded state, last exit status, and log freshness, and flags anything older than a day or not successful.
  2. Backup scripts that wait or retry for network connectivity before failing.
  3. A scheduled restore test, so that “backed up” means “restored at least once.”
  4. Secret scanning on every commit to the dotfiles repository.
  5. A second exercise of the reinstall runbook, to find the parts that were specific to the first machine by accident.
  6. A firewall item in the audit list for every machine, with the check to run on the Macs as well as on the Linux hosts.

Wrapping Up

The audit the hub recommends was worth doing, though not in the shape expected. Every control the threat model named held. The failures lived around those controls: credentials with too little coverage or too much, OAuth grants whose fate is shared across machines, backups that succeeded while covering less than intended, and the slow drift of everything near a correct configuration, from a router-assigned address to a tool one machine never installed. None of these were configuration errors when they were configured. All of them were found by checking, and none by an alert.

Takeaways:

  • Read backup logs and exit statuses on every machine; a schedule is not evidence.
  • Before revoking any credential or grant, know everything that depends on it.
  • Verify every fix on every machine it touches, including the ones that run a different operating system.
  • Prefer addresses and configurations that cannot change underneath you, and know every file that names a machine.
  • Record each finding in writing the day it is fixed.

See Also

Security series:

  1. Security Foundations for a Multi-Machine Research Fleet
  2. Setting Up pass: a Unix Password Manager
  3. Secrets Management for the Workflow Construct
  4. Migrating Off Dropbox: Beyond Dotfiles
  5. Research Backup Architecture: Borg, Cloud Copies, and Time Machine
  6. A Home Server for a Five-Machine Research Fleet
  7. Object Storage for Research Data: The Layer Git Cannot Hold
  8. Running the Quarterly Security Audit for the First Time: What Actually Broke (this post)

External references:

  • BorgBackup documentation
  • rclone documentation
  • GitHub CLI manual
  • Tailscale documentation
  • Samba vfs_fruit manual page

Reproducibility

This post contains no executable analysis. The commands shown are the checks and the lock line used on the fleet during the audit. Environment at the time of writing: macOS 26.6 on the three Macs, Linux Mint 22.3 on the Linux laptop and Linux Mint on the home server, Borg 1.4.5, rclone 1.75, flock 0.4.0 (Homebrew). Finding 18 was checked on 2026-10-11 against the running laptop (firewall state before and after, and each way in afterwards). Exact command output, host names beyond the machine names, and addresses are omitted deliberately.

Let’s Connect

Questions, suggestions, or corrections are welcome.

  • GitHub: rgt47
  • Twitter/X: @rgt47
  • LinkedIn: Ronald Glenn Thomas
  • Email: Contact form

I would like to hear from you if:

  • You find an error, or a better approach to anything in this series.
  • You run a small research fleet and have found where this design breaks.
  • You want to compare notes on backups, secrets, or reproducible research infrastructure.

item.title: A Home Server for a Five-Machine Research Fleet
item.dc:creator: Ronald G. Thomas
item.description:
WarningDraft

This post is a work in progress and may change.

Introduction

Five machines are enough to need a center. This post describes the one in our fleet: a 2016 MacBook Pro, retired from daily use, running Linux Mint, and serving the other four machines as their backup destination and as a home for the few things that must not leave the house.

Note

Part 6 of the security series; start with Security Foundations for a Multi-Machine Research Fleet for the overview.

The server is called mercury. The other machines are julia (the primary workstation), athena (a laptop, and the only Mac running Time Machine), joe (a secondary Mac), and zeus (a Linux laptop). The backup policy that runs against mercury is the subject of Research Backup Architecture; this post is about the machine itself: what it does, how it is reached, how it is protected, and the configuration details that took more than one attempt to get right.

Motivations

  • Four machines backing up nightly need a destination that is always on, inside the house, and under our control.
  • athena’s Time Machine disk was a USB drive that had to be plugged into athena; a network share removes that dependency.
  • Some repositories hold material that is forbidden from ever having a GitHub remote. They still need an off-machine copy.
  • An old laptop was already on hand, with 16 GB of memory and a 1 TB internal SSD, and a battery that rides out short power cuts.
  • Every service added to a machine on the LAN is a new way in. The server needed to be closed by default and opened deliberately.

Objectives

  • Document the server’s roles and, as importantly, what it does not do.
  • Show how a laptop is made to behave like a server: no sleep on lid close, no suspend, full-disk encryption.
  • Explain why scripted connections use Tailscale addresses and only the Time Machine share uses the LAN.
  • Give the firewall policy, the external SSD setup, and the Samba share configuration as trimmed, real excerpts.
  • Record the failures, each of which produced a rule worth keeping.

What Is the Home Server For?

mercury has five roles and several deliberate non-roles.

Role Mechanism Clients
Borg repository host one repository per machine under /srv/backup, append-only access julia, athena, joe, zeus
Time Machine share Samba with vfs_fruit, on an external SSD athena
Remote of last resort bare git repositories under /srv/git any machine
Research data area plain directory under /srv/data, fetched, not synced any machine
Simulation host (one of two) rootless Podman containers and a one-at-a-time job queue; see Offloading R Simulations to a Home Server julia, athena, joe

The fifth role was added last and is the one that sits least comfortably with the others: it runs other people’s code, here the author’s own simulation scripts, on the machine that holds the backups. The limitations section returns to this, and the second host in the fleet exists partly so that heavy or untrusted work has somewhere else to go.

The server’s own home directory and its /srv/git and /srv/data folders are backed up nightly in the other direction, to a Borg repository on julia, so the backup destination is itself backed up.

What it does not do matters as much:

  • It runs no file-sync daemon. The fleet left Dropbox precisely to stop every machine holding a mutable copy of everything; see Migrating Off Dropbox.
  • It is not reachable from the internet. Remote access goes through Tailscale.
  • It does not hold the backup passphrases. It stores four encrypted Borg repositories it cannot read.
  • It does not hold the password store’s remote, which lives on one of the Macs; see Setting Up pass.
  • It does not yet run an object store. Whether one is worth running for research data is argued in Object Storage for Research Data.

Prerequisites

  • A spare machine with enough disk for every client’s backups plus growth. mercury has a 1 TB internal SSD for the Borg repositories and a separate 1 TB USB SSD for Time Machine.
  • Linux (here Linux Mint 22.3) installed with full-disk encryption (LUKS). Encryption at rest is a fleet-wide control; see the series overview.
  • Tailscale installed on the server and on every client.
  • borgbackup, samba, and ufw from the distribution’s packages.
  • A login on the server for the account that owns the backups.

A Laptop That Behaves Like a Server

A laptop wants to sleep. Three settings stop it.

The lid switch is ignored whether or not the machine is on power, through a drop-in for systemd-logind:

# /etc/systemd/logind.conf.d/99-mercury-no-sleep.conf
# mercury is the LAN hub; it must not sleep.
[Login]
HandleLidSwitch=ignore
HandleLidSwitchExternalPower=ignore
HandleLidSwitchDocked=ignore
HandleSuspendKey=ignore
HandleHibernateKey=ignore
IdleAction=ignore

The sleep and suspend targets are masked, so nothing (a desktop power applet, an idle timer) can suspend the machine behind the drop-in’s back:

sudo systemctl mask sleep.target suspend.target
systemctl is-enabled sleep.target suspend.target
# masked
# masked

The remaining hardware realities are less tractable:

  • No wired network. The 2016 MacBook Pro has no Ethernet port, and mercury runs on Wi-Fi. It has two Wi-Fi adapters, the built-in one and a USB adapter, both joined to the home network. That detail caused one of the Samba failures described below.
  • A battery is not a UPS. The battery carries the machine through a short outage, but there is no clean-shutdown trigger and the battery is old.
  • LUKS needs a passphrase at boot. An unattended reboot stops at the unlock prompt until someone types it. This is the server’s equivalent of the FileVault behavior described in the series overview, and it is the price of encryption at rest.

Addressing: Tailscale for Scripts, the LAN for Samba

Every scripted connection to mercury uses its Tailscale address. Only Time Machine, through Samba, uses the LAN. (The simulation client was briefly an exception: on two of the Macs it defaulted to the server’s .local multicast name. That name depends on multicast DNS, which failed on the first lookup after a quiet period on both Macs tested (then worked), so all three Macs now default to the Tailscale alias, and the .local aliases are used only when typed. The cost is that submitting a job needs Tailscale running even at home.)

The reason is a failure. mercury originally appeared in each client’s SSH configuration under its LAN address, which the home router assigns by DHCP. After a reboot in late September 2026 the router handed mercury new addresses. Nothing announced the change: the Borg jobs on athena, joe, and zeus simply timed out every night until a status check found them. julia was unaffected because its configuration already used the Tailscale address, which does not change when the LAN does.

The fix had a second lesson in it. Each client names the server in two places: the general ~/.ssh/config, and a separate SSH config that the Borg script passes with ssh -F so that only the restricted backup key is offered. Correcting the first file left the backups failing; only correcting the second fixed them. The client side is described in the backup post; on this side, the rule is simple:

  • Scripts address the server by its Tailscale address (or its Tailscale name), never by a DHCP-assigned LAN address.
  • Services that must be reached over the LAN, here the Samba share, should have their LAN address reserved in the router, so that a reboot cannot move them.
  • When the address of a machine changes, search every client for every file that names it before declaring the fix done.

One more addressing detail affects Samba clients. On the Macs, mercury.local (multicast DNS) resolves to both Wi-Fi adapters’ IPv4 addresses and to two IPv6 link-local addresses. A client that tries them one at a time can spend tens of seconds on the addresses that do not answer before reaching one that does.

The Firewall: Default Deny

Before Samba was added, mercury ran with its firewall installed but inactive, relying on the home router and on the restricted Borg keys. Adding a second network-facing service was the point at which that stopped being defensible. ufw now denies all incoming connections by default and opens three things:

# Policy as configured, shown as the commands that produce it.
# The LAN subnet is shown as a documentation range.
sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing
sudo ufw allow in on tailscale0
sudo ufw allow from 192.0.2.0/24 to any port 22 proto tcp
sudo ufw allow from 192.0.2.0/24 to any port 445 proto tcp
sudo ufw enable

The Tailscale interface is trusted as a whole because every machine on the tailnet is one of ours and the Borg traffic arrives that way. SSH and Samba are additionally reachable from the LAN subnet and from nowhere else. Enabling a firewall over SSH is the moment to be careful: allow SSH first, keep the existing session open, and test a second login before closing the first.

Samba applies its own restriction on top of the firewall, so a mistake in either layer alone does not expose the share:

# /etc/samba/smb.conf, [grey] share (excerpt)
hosts allow = 192.0.2.0/24 127.0.0.1
hosts deny = 0.0.0.0/0
valid users = <backup-user>
guest ok = no

The Borg Repository Host

Each client has its own repository under /srv/backup/<machine>, and its own SSH key. On the server, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys pins each key to one command and one repository:

command="/usr/local/bin/borg serve --append-only \
  --restrict-to-repository /srv/backup/athena",restrict ssh-ed25519 ...

(Shown wrapped; in the file it is one line per key.) The effect:

  • A client key cannot open a shell, read another machine’s repository, or delete existing archives. The worst an attacker holding one key can do is add data to that one repository.
  • Because access is append-only, clients cannot prune. Pruning runs quarterly and by hand, with the passphrase typed at the time, because the server holding the repositories never holds their passphrases. The policy and its reasoning are in Research Backup Architecture.
  • The repositories live on the internal SSD, not on the external Time Machine disk, so the two backup tiers do not share a device.

The External SSD

athena’s Time Machine disk, a 1 TB Samsung T7 USB SSD, moved from athena’s desk to mercury.

ext4, After an HFS+ Experiment Failed

The first format was HFS+, chosen deliberately: HFS+ can be read natively by both Linux and macOS, so if mercury died the disk could be plugged straight into a Mac. No guide documents HFS+ under Samba as a supported Time Machine target, and the experiment showed why. The drive dropped off the USB bus in the middle of a write; the Linux HFS+ checker, fsck.hfsplus, then crashed on the drive’s long device path (a known bug, Launchpad #1450760), so the volume could not be verified. A Time Machine destination that cannot be checked after an unclean disconnect is not one to rely on.

The disk was reformatted as ext4, which the Samba Time Machine guides do document. The cost is real and accepted: macOS cannot read the disk directly, so recovering it without mercury needs a Linux machine or a third-party ext4 driver.

Mounting: nofail and a Mountpoint Guard

# /etc/fstab (UUID shortened)
UUID=...  /media/grey  ext4  defaults,noatime,nofail,\
  x-systemd.device-timeout=10s  0  2

nofail with a short device timeout lets mercury boot normally when the disk is unplugged; without it, a missing USB drive drops a Linux machine into emergency mode at boot, which on a headless server means a trip to the keyboard.

The opposite failure is quieter and worse: with the disk absent, /media/grey is an empty directory on the internal SSD, and Samba would happily serve it. Time Machine would then fill the server’s system disk. The share refuses to start a session unless the disk is actually mounted:

# /etc/samba/smb.conf, [grey] share (excerpt)
root preexec = /usr/bin/mountpoint -q /media/grey
root preexec close = yes

root preexec close = yes turns a failing pre-exec command into a refused connection.

TRIM over USB

Linux does not pass TRIM to most USB SSDs by default; the SCSI layer reports the device’s provisioning mode as full, and fstrim answers that discard is not supported. A udev rule switches this drive model to unmap whenever it appears:

# /etc/udev/rules.d/50-grey-trim.rules
ACTION=="add|change", ATTRS{idVendor}=="04e8", \
  ATTRS{idProduct}=="4001", SUBSYSTEM=="scsi_disk", \
  ATTR{provisioning_mode}="unmap"

(Shown wrapped; udev needs one line.) Check it and trim:

cat /sys/block/sda/device/scsi_disk/*/provisioning_mode
# unmap
sudo fstrim -v /media/grey

The first fstrim after the reformat released the whole drive, 915.6 GiB. The vendor and product IDs come from lsusb; the rule is specific to one drive model, which is intended, since forcing unmap on a bridge that does not support it can cause errors.

The Time Machine Share

The share definition, trimmed of comments:

[grey]
   comment = Time Machine backup for athena (ext4 on mercury)
   path = /media/grey
   root preexec = /usr/bin/mountpoint -q /media/grey
   root preexec close = yes
   vfs objects = fruit streams_xattr
   fruit:time machine = yes
   fruit:time machine max size = 966367641600
   fruit:metadata = stream
   fruit:model = MacSamba
   hosts allow = 192.0.2.0/24 127.0.0.1
   hosts deny = 0.0.0.0/0
   valid users = <backup-user>
   guest ok = no
   read only = no
   create mask = 0600
   directory mask = 0700

Notes on the choices:

  • fruit:time machine = yes makes the share advertise itself as a Time Machine destination; max size caps it below the disk’s capacity (here 900 GiB) so Time Machine prunes before the disk fills.
  • The Samba account has its own password, set with smbpasswd, separate from the Linux login and from the password store.
  • Encryption is the client’s job: Time Machine encrypts the backup only if Encrypt Backup is chosen when the destination is added. The server stores an encrypted sparse bundle it cannot read. The first attempt here was added without encryption and had to be deleted and restarted; the procedure is in the backup post.

Binding to Interfaces, and Waiting for Them

The share was configured to listen only on chosen interfaces:

[global]
   interfaces = lo wlp2s0 wlx9cefd5fb70dd
   bind interfaces only = yes

This is good practice (Samba does not answer on the Tailscale interface at all) and it caused two failures.

Samba started before the network. At boot, smbd started before the USB Wi-Fi adapter had an address, bound only to loopback, and never retried. From the LAN the share simply refused connections, while the disk itself was mounted and writable. A systemd drop-in makes Samba wait for the network:

# /etc/systemd/system/smbd.service.d/wait-for-network.conf
[Unit]
Wants=network-online.target
After=network-online.target

This only helps if a wait-online service is enabled for the network manager in use (NetworkManager-wait-online.service on Mint); check it, or network-online.target is reached immediately.

Samba listened on one of two adapters. The original line named only the USB adapter. Because mercury.local resolves to both adapters, a Mac reaching the built-in adapter’s address was refused. Listing both adapters fixed it. Confirm what Samba is actually listening on, rather than what the configuration says:

ss -tln | grep ':445 '

The general lesson: a service bound to named interfaces on a machine whose interfaces come up late or change needs both a boot ordering dependency and a check of its real listening sockets after every reboot.

Research Data and Git Remotes of Last Resort

Two smaller roles round out the server.

/srv/git holds bare repositories for work that must never have a GitHub remote, such as repositories holding subject-level clinical data. A clone over SSH (git clone mercury:/srv/git/<name>.git) gives them an off-machine copy without a third party.

/srv/data holds research data that is not in git. Clients fetch from it; they do not each keep a synchronized, mutable copy, which is the model that produced dozens of conflict copies under Dropbox. One practical warning from seeding it: macOS ships openrsync as rsync, and during the migration it twice exited with status 0 while silently omitting thousands of files. Seed with a tar stream, or install GNU rsync, and count files on both sides afterward.

Whether this directory should become an S3-compatible object store, with content hashes and versioning, is argued in Object Storage for Research Data. Every lesson in this post (stable addressing, a firewall first, waiting for the network at boot, checking real listening sockets) would apply to that service unchanged.

Verification

Run on the server after any change and after every reboot:

# Encrypted root and the SSD mounted read-write
lsblk -o NAME,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINT
findmnt -n -o TARGET,FSTYPE,OPTIONS /media/grey

# TRIM enabled on the USB SSD
cat /sys/block/sda/device/scsi_disk/*/provisioning_mode

# Samba up and listening on the LAN adapters, not just loopback
systemctl is-active smbd
ss -tln | grep ':445 '

# Firewall active with the expected rules
sudo ufw status verbose

# Sleep impossible
systemctl is-enabled sleep.target suspend.target

From a client:

# macOS: the share answers on each LAN address
nc -z -G 5 <server-lan-address> 445

# Borg: the restricted key reaches only borg serve
ssh -F ~/.borg/ssh_config mercury true
# expected: a borg usage message, not a shell

The last check is the one that proves the restriction: if true runs, the forced command is not in effect.

Things to Watch Out For

  1. DHCP addresses move. Address the server by its Tailscale address in scripts, and reserve LAN addresses for LAN services.
  2. Server names live in more than one file. A restricted-key setup has its own SSH config; search every client for every file that names the server.
  3. A status check must cover every machine. The first check after the address change looked only at the Macs; zeus’s backups had been failing just as long and were found a day later.
  4. bind interfaces only plus a late network means loopback only. Order Samba after network-online.target and verify with ss.
  5. An unmounted mount point is an empty directory. Guard network shares with mountpoint -q, and use nofail so a missing disk does not stop boot.
  6. USB SSDs do not TRIM by default on Linux. Set provisioning_mode with a udev rule scoped to the drive model.
  7. HFS+ on Linux is not a recovery format. Without a working checker, cross-platform readability does not help.
  8. Enabling a firewall over SSH can lock you out. Allow SSH before ufw enable, and test a second session.
  9. LUKS and unattended reboots do not mix. Plan for someone to unlock the server after power loss or a kernel update.

What Did We Learn?

Lessons Learned

  • The failures were silent. Borg timed out, Samba listened on loopback, and nothing reported either. Each was found by reading a log or checking a socket, not by an alert.
  • Stable names beat convenient ones. The LAN address was easy to type and wrong a week later; the Tailscale address has not changed.
  • Defense in depth is cheap here. The firewall, Samba’s hosts allow, a separate Samba password, and client-side encryption each cover a mistake in the others.
  • Experiments on a backup target need an exit. HFS+ was a reasonable hypothesis, tested, and abandoned the first time it could not be verified.
  • A server that cannot read what it stores is a smaller target, for confidentiality. Holding encrypted repositories without their passphrases keeps a compromise of mercury from becoming a compromise of every machine’s data. It does not protect availability: Borg’s append-only mode is enforced by the restricted keys, not by file permissions, so code running as the account that owns the repositories could delete the backups even though it could not read them. Simulation jobs originally ran as that account, which made the server’s second role a route to its first. They now run as a separate unprivileged account (described in Offloading R Simulations to a Home Server), whose file permissions give it no access to the repositories.

Limitations

  • One server is one point of failure for the Borg tier; the cloud copies and the server’s own backup to julia mitigate this, but a restore onto replacement hardware has not yet been rehearsed.
  • Wi-Fi is the only network path, and the server’s throughput sets the pace of large first backups (a full Time Machine baseline runs for many hours).
  • The Time Machine share is treated as a convenience tier. athena’s research data also exists in Borg and in its cloud copies; the share itself has no second copy.
  • There is no automated alerting on the server’s services; the verification list above is run by hand.
  • Simulation jobs run as a dedicated account, simrun, with no sudo and no access to the backup repositories, in rootless containers under that account. A job can still fill the disk or keep the CPU busy, so a runaway job affects availability, and simrun owns the simulation data store. Mercury remains the slower of the two simulation hosts, with four threads.

Opportunities for Improvement

  • A USB Ethernet adapter and a wired link to the router.
  • A small UPS with a shutdown trigger, so power loss ends in a clean shutdown rather than a drained battery.
  • A daily check that reports the services’ status and listening sockets, alongside the backup status check recommended in the backup post.
  • A scheduled restore test from both the Borg repositories and the Time Machine share.
  • An object store for research data, if the argument in post 7 holds up in practice.

Wrapping Up

A home server for a small fleet does not need to be new or fast. It needs to stay awake, keep a stable address, refuse everything it was not asked to accept, and fail loudly enough to be noticed. The old MacBook Pro does the first three well. The fourth is still done by reading logs, which is the reason the series keeps returning to monitoring.

Takeaways:

  • Address servers by a stable overlay name (Tailscale), not by a DHCP-assigned LAN address.
  • Start with a default-deny firewall and open each service deliberately, then restrict it again at the service.
  • Store backups the server cannot decrypt, through keys that can only append.
  • For Samba on Linux: ext4, a mountpoint guard, nofail, TRIM via udev, and a boot ordering dependency on the network.
  • After every reboot, check what is actually listening, not what the configuration intends.

See Also

Security series:

  1. Security Foundations for a Multi-Machine Research Fleet
  2. Setting Up pass: a Unix Password Manager
  3. Secrets Management for the Workflow Construct
  4. Migrating Off Dropbox: Beyond Dotfiles
  5. Research Backup Architecture: Borg, Cloud Copies, and Time Machine
  6. A Home Server for a Five-Machine Research Fleet (this post)
  7. Object Storage for Research Data: The Layer Git Cannot Hold
  8. Running the Quarterly Security Audit for the First Time: What Actually Broke

External references:

  • Samba vfs_fruit manual page: https://www.samba.org/samba/docs/current/man-html/vfs_fruit.8.html
  • BorgBackup documentation, borg serve and append-only mode: https://borgbackup.readthedocs.io/en/stable/usage/serve.html
  • Tailscale documentation: https://tailscale.com/kb
  • Ubuntu ufw documentation: https://help.ubuntu.com/community/UFW
  • Launchpad bug #1450760, fsck.hfsplus crash: https://bugs.launchpad.net/bugs/1450760
  • ArchWiki, Solid state drive, TRIM on USB devices: https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/Solid_state_drive

Reproducibility

What was checked. The configuration excerpts (logind drop-in, masked sleep targets, Samba [global] binding and [grey] share, the smbd drop-in, the fstab line, the udev rule, the Borg forced commands) were read from the running server on 2026-10-01 and are shown trimmed, with the LAN subnet replaced by a documentation range and the filesystem UUID removed. The firewall policy is given as the commands that produce it, from the build notes; ufw status output was not captured for this post. Listening sockets, the mount, and TRIM were verified on the server; port 445 on both LAN addresses was verified from athena. The simulation role was added after those checks (2026-10-03 onward); for this post, only the file ownership behind the limitation above was read from the server on 2026-10-12: the Borg repositories and the Time Machine drive are owned by the backup account, which is in the sudo group. The separate simrun account was created on 2026-10-15; that it has no sudo membership and that the repositories are mode 0750 for another owner and group was read from the account listing and file modes, not tested by trying to read them as simrun. The simulation design itself is verified in its own post.

Versions. Server: Linux Mint 22.3, kernel 7.0.0-31, Samba 4.19.5, BorgBackup 1.4.5, Tailscale 1.102.4. Clients: macOS 26.

Not done. A restore from the Time Machine share, and a full restore from Borg onto replacement hardware, have not been tested.

AI involvement in this post: drafting was AI-assisted, and the configuration was read and verified with assistance. The design decisions and editorial judgment are the author’s.

Let’s Connect

Questions, suggestions, or corrections are welcome.

item.title: Object Storage for Research Data: The Layer Git Cannot Hold
item.dc:creator: Ronald G. Thomas
item.description:
WarningDraft

This post is a work in progress and may change.

A repository never edits a box; it accessions a new one, and the old number still means what it always meant.

Introduction

Leaving a sync daemon settles where code goes: into git repositories. It does not settle where research data goes. The usual answer, some mixture of a shared folder and a habit of copying, carries forward the property that made the sync daemon painful in the first place: the same mutable file existing in several places at once, with conflict copies, silent overwrites, and no way to say which version produced a given table.

Note

Part 7 of the security series; start with Security Foundations for a Multi-Machine Research Fleet for the overview.

This post argues that the question is malformed. Asking how to synchronize research data presumes the data should be mutable and replicated. An object store declines that premise: data is written once under a key, never modified, and fetched on demand. Nothing has to agree with anything, because nothing changes. A laptop stops being a replica and becomes a cache.

The post is a design argument with a tested worked example, not a deployment report. No object store runs on the fleet’s home server today. A section below states what the fleet does instead and what would justify the change.

Motivations

  • Every sync mechanism compared in the post on leaving Dropbox is one-way, conflict-prone, quota-limited, or all three when applied to data.
  • A reproducible compendium pins its code, environment, and package versions, then says nothing machine-checkable about which bytes of data it consumed.
  • Students arriving in a lab need a rule for where data goes that does not depend on remembering to copy something.
  • Restricted data under a data use agreement needs access that can be revoked centrally, which copies on laptops cannot offer.

Objectives

  1. Explain what an object store is, separately from the file-sharing services it superficially resembles.
  2. Give a manifest-and-fetch pattern small enough to adopt in an afternoon, tested end to end.
  3. Show where the pattern fits in a zzcollab compendium, including the hash-linked provenance chain from a rendered report to the exact bytes, where that chain is weak, and whether it is a blockchain.
  4. Give a tested setup for a self-hosted store that enforces immutability, and the operational conditions for running it on a home server.
  5. Compare costs and say when the pattern is the wrong shape for the work.

What is an Object Store?

An object store is not a folder, and the most common way to misuse one is to mount it and treat it as though it were.

The model is a flat namespace of immutable blobs. You put an object under a key and get it back by that key; no operation edits it in place. The interface is HTTP rather than a filesystem: no partial writes, no locking, no rename, and no directories except as a convention about slashes in key names.

Two API families implement the model. Amazon S3 is the commercially dominant one, and its interface is the de facto standard that SeaweedFS, Garage, Ceph, Backblaze, and Wasabi all speak. OpenStack Swift is older and still common in academic and national-laboratory deployments, where a bucket is called a container. The architecture is identical; only the wire protocol and tooling differ, which matters when an institutional service turns out to speak Swift.

Three properties follow from immutability, and they carry the whole argument:

  • No conflict, because no concurrent modification. A corrected extract is not an edit; it is a new object under a new key.
  • A key plus a content hash is a durable citation. If an analysis records the hash of what it read, the claim ‘this table came from that data’ is checkable years later without trusting a filename.
  • Access is centrally governed. Revoking one credential removes access everywhere at once. No folder-sharing arrangement can promise that, because copies have already left.

What it is not

It is not a backup system. A mistaken write under a new key is still a mistaken write, and lifecycle rules that expire old versions will expire the one you wanted. Backup stays a separate concern; see the backup post.

It is not a filesystem. Tools that make it look like one (s3fs and its relatives) reintroduce every problem the model removes. Fetch explicitly.

It is not, on its own, a data management plan. It is a substrate that makes a good plan expressible.

When a Store Earns Its Keep

The fleet described in this series does not run an object store. Research data that is too large or too restricted for git lives in a plain directory on the home server, and workstations fetch from it. Code is in git; working copies of projects are protected by Borg, cloud copies, and Time Machine.

That arrangement is adequate while one person produces and consumes each dataset. It has none of the properties argued for here: no versioning, no write-once enforcement, and no read-only identity that a collaborator could be given. The manifest pattern below does not need a store to be useful; it was tested against a plain directory exposed as an rclone remote, and it adds verification and provenance there too. What a store adds is enforcement on the server side.

The deployment is justified when any of the following becomes true:

  • A second analyst needs the canonical dataset. At that point ‘everyone agrees not to overwrite it’ stops being a control.
  • A data use agreement requires revocable access or audited custody that copies on laptops cannot provide.
  • A result must be defended later by showing the exact input bytes, which needs both the manifest’s hash and a store that cannot destroy the version it names.
  • Datasets outgrow the plain directory’s informal discipline: many versions, several projects reading the same extract, or derived data expensive enough to publish rather than regenerate.

Until then, adopting the manifest and the read-through helper costs an afternoon and moves nothing.

Prerequisites

  • A project laid out as a zzcollab compendium, or any layout with a raw-data directory excluded from git.
  • rclone (tested with 1.75), R with the digest and tinytest packages, bash, and shasum.
  • For the store walkthrough: SeaweedFS (tested with 4.46 and 4.47) and the AWS CLI, on a machine you control.
  • Credentials kept in pass and loaded on demand, as described in the secrets post.

The Pattern

The pattern is four moves: data leaves the project directory, a manifest takes its place in git, a build step fetches exactly what the manifest names and checks it, and the analysis refuses to read anything the manifest does not vouch for.

Every listing in this section is read at render time from a small working example stored beside this post (analysis/scripts/manifest-pattern/). Two test scripts in the same folder ran it end to end, one against a local directory and one against an S3 endpoint with object lock; the results are tabulated at the end of the section. The layout follows a zzcollab compendium (analysis/data/raw_data/, analysis/scripts/, R/, inst/tinytest/), for reasons the next section gives.

Move 1: the manifest

The compendium tracks a small tab-separated file naming each dataset, where it lives, its content hash, and the terms under which it may be used. The example ships with only the header row; the tests publish into it. Populated, it looks like this (the codebook row is illustrative):

# analysis/data/manifest.tsv
name              remote  container  object      sha256     terms
trial_extract_v3  lab     trial      ext_v3.csv  77cad0...  synthetic
codebook_v3       lab     trial      cb_v3.csv   41cd88...  synthetic

The location is written as remote, container, and object rather than as one s3:// URL on purpose. A protocol scheme inside the key bakes one vendor into a file meant to outlive the storage choice. The remote name resolves through the client’s configuration, which is where protocol details belong.

Two columns carry the argument. The sha256 is the dataset’s identity; the key only says where to look, and a later section shows why that distinction matters. The terms column puts the license or data use restriction on the same line as the hash, so it travels into every provenance record the analysis writes.

The file is a few hundred bytes, diffs cleanly, and reviews in a pull request. It is append-only in practice: a corrected extract is published under a new name and key, which adds a row, and the analysis moves to it by changing the one line that names the dataset. Both halves appear in the same pull request.

Move 2: fetch what the manifest names, and nothing else

The fetch belongs in the build, not in anyone’s memory. The Makefile is deliberately thin; each data target hands off to one script that reads the manifest.

Makefile
SHELL := /bin/bash
.SHELLFLAGS := -eu -c

RAW_DATA_DIR ?= analysis/data/raw_data
export RAW_DATA_DIR

.PHONY: fetch-data verify-data publish-data analysis report test

fetch-data: ## Pull every manifest dataset not already cached, verified
    bash tools/data-manifest.sh fetch

verify-data: ## Check local copies against the manifest's sha256 column
    bash tools/data-manifest.sh verify

# make publish-data NAME=trial_extract_v4 FILE=ext_v4.csv \
#   CONTAINER=trial OBJECT=ext_v4.csv TERMS='DUA 2026-014'
publish-data: ## Upload a new dataset and append its manifest row
    bash tools/data-manifest.sh publish \
      "$(NAME)" "$(FILE)" "$(CONTAINER)" "$(OBJECT)" "$(TERMS)"

analysis: fetch-data
    Rscript analysis/scripts/01_prepare_data.R

report: analysis ## Render the report and register its hash
    Rscript analysis/scripts/02_report.R

test:
    Rscript -e "tinytest::run_test_dir('inst/tinytest')"

What matters about the script is what each subcommand refuses to do.

  • fetch takes every key from the manifest, so changing the manifest changes what is downloaded.
  • A verified local copy is a cache hit. If the file is present and its hash matches, nothing is transferred.
  • Bytes that fail the hash are deleted before anything can read them, and the target fails, naming the dataset.
  • verify derives its expectations from the same sha256 column, so there is no second checksum file to drift.
  • publish hashes the bytes being uploaded, at write time, refuses a name already in the manifest or a key already in the store, reads the object back and hashes it again, and only then appends the row.
NoteFull listing: tools/data-manifest.sh 
tools/data-manifest.sh
#!/bin/bash
# data-manifest.sh -- fetch, verify, and publish datasets named in
# analysis/data/manifest.tsv. The manifest is the single source of truth:
# the key says where to fetch from, the sha256 says what must arrive.
#
#   data-manifest.sh verify
#   data-manifest.sh fetch
#   data-manifest.sh publish NAME FILE CONTAINER OBJECT [TERMS]
set -euo pipefail

MANIFEST=${MANIFEST:-analysis/data/manifest.tsv}
RAW_DATA_DIR=${RAW_DATA_DIR:-analysis/data/raw_data}
REMOTE=${DATA_REMOTE:-lab}

sha256_of() { shasum -a 256 "$1" | cut -d' ' -f1; }

# Rows only: skip the header and comment lines.
rows() { grep -v '^#' "$MANIFEST" | tail -n +2; }

local_path() { printf '%s/%s/%s' "$RAW_DATA_DIR" "$1" "$2"; }

verify_one() {
  local name=$1 path=$2 want=$3 got
  if [ ! -f "$path" ]; then
    echo "MISSING  $name  ($path; run 'make fetch-data')"
    return 1
  fi
  got=$(sha256_of "$path")
  if [ "$got" != "$want" ]; then
    echo "FAILED   $name  expected ${want:0:12} got ${got:0:12}"
    return 1
  fi
  echo "OK       $name  ${want:0:12}"
}

cmd_verify() {
  local bad=0 name remote container object sha terms
  while IFS=$'\t' read -r name remote container object sha terms; do
    verify_one "$name" "$(local_path "$container" "$object")" "$sha" \
      || bad=$((bad + 1))
  done < <(rows)
  [ "$bad" -eq 0 ] || { echo "$bad dataset(s) failed verification"; exit 1; }
}

cmd_fetch() {
  local bad=0 name remote container object sha terms path
  while IFS=$'\t' read -r name remote container object sha terms; do
    path=$(local_path "$container" "$object")
    # A verified local copy is a cache hit; repeated builds cost nothing.
    if [ -f "$path" ] && [ "$(sha256_of "$path")" = "$sha" ]; then
      echo "CACHED   $name"
      continue
    fi
    mkdir -p "$(dirname "$path")"
    # </dev/null: the loop's stdin is the manifest; nothing may eat it.
    rclone copyto "$remote:$container/$object" "$path" </dev/null
    if ! verify_one "$name" "$path" "$sha"; then
      # Never leave bytes the manifest does not vouch for where an
      # analysis could read them.
      rm -f "$path"
      bad=$((bad + 1))
    fi
  done < <(rows)
  [ "$bad" -eq 0 ] || { echo "$bad dataset(s) failed on fetch"; exit 1; }
}

cmd_publish() {
  local name=${1:?name} file=${2:?file} container=${3:?container}
  local object=${4:?object} terms=${5:-unspecified} sha remote_sha
  [ -f "$file" ] || { echo "no such file: $file"; exit 1; }
  if rows | cut -f1 | grep -qx "$name"; then
    echo "refusing: '$name' is already in $MANIFEST; publish a new name"
    exit 1
  fi
  if [ -n "$(rclone lsf "$REMOTE:$container/$object" 2>/dev/null)" ]; then
    echo "refusing: $REMOTE:$container/$object already exists; keys are"
    echo "write-once, so give the new version a new object name"
    exit 1
  fi
  # Hash at write time, from the bytes being published, not later from
  # whatever copy someone happens to read first.
  sha=$(sha256_of "$file")
  rclone copyto "$file" "$REMOTE:$container/$object"
  remote_sha=$(rclone cat "$REMOTE:$container/$object" | shasum -a 256 \
    | cut -d' ' -f1)
  if [ "$remote_sha" != "$sha" ]; then
    echo "upload verification failed for $object"; exit 1
  fi
  printf '%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' \
    "$name" "$REMOTE" "$container" "$object" "$sha" "$terms" >> "$MANIFEST"
  echo "published $name -> $REMOTE:$container/$object ${sha:0:12}"
}

case "${1:-}" in
  verify)  cmd_verify ;;
  fetch)   cmd_fetch ;;
  publish) shift; cmd_publish "$@" ;;
  *) echo "usage: $0 verify | fetch |"
     echo "       $0 publish NAME FILE CONTAINER OBJECT [TERMS]"
     exit 2 ;;
esac

rclone is the client because the remote is named lab and nothing in the script says which protocol lab speaks. rclone has native backends for S3, Swift, and roughly forty others, so the same build step works against a self-hosted gateway, an institutional Swift service, a commercial bucket, or a plain directory. The two tests make the point: the same unmodified script ran against a local directory and against an S3 endpoint, and only the definition of lab differed. Credentials for either backend can be supplied through environment variables from pass rather than written to rclone.conf.

Move 3: read only through the manifest

Verification in the build protects the build. It does not protect a script run directly from the console, which is how most analysis scripts are run. So the analysis never opens a raw file by path; it asks for a dataset by name.

analysis/scripts/01_prepare_data.R
source(here::here('R', 'data_manifest.R'))

trial <- read.csv(use_dataset('trial_extract_v3'))
stopifnot(nrow(trial) > 0, all(c('arm', 'outcome') %in% names(trial)))

by_arm <- trial |>
  aggregate(outcome ~ arm, data = _, FUN = mean)

derived <- here::here('analysis', 'data', 'derived_data')
dir.create(derived, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
write.csv(by_arm, file.path(derived, 'outcome_by_arm.csv'),
          row.names = FALSE)
write_provenance(file.path(derived, 'outcome_by_arm.provenance.tsv'))

use_dataset() looks the name up in the manifest, hashes the local copy, and returns the path only if the two agree, recording the read (name, key, hash, terms, time). write_provenance() writes that record beside the derived output, with the full commit hash of the code and a flag saying whether tracked files had uncommitted changes. From the test run, with the remote, terms, and read_at columns omitted and hashes shortened:

NoteFull listing: R/data_manifest.R 
R/data_manifest.R
.provenance <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
.provenance$log <- NULL

#' Read the project data manifest
#'
#' @param path Path to the tab-separated manifest.
#' @return A data frame with one character column per manifest field.
#' @export
read_data_manifest <- function(
    path = here::here('analysis', 'data', 'manifest.tsv')) {
  utils::read.delim(path, colClasses = 'character', comment.char = '#')
}

#' Path to a verified local copy of a manifest dataset
#'
#' Looks up `name` in the manifest, checks the local copy's sha256
#' against the manifest entry, records the read in the session
#' provenance log, and returns the path. It errors rather than return
#' a file the manifest does not vouch for.
#'
#' @param name Dataset name, as in the manifest's `name` column.
#' @param manifest A manifest data frame from [read_data_manifest()].
#' @param raw_dir Directory that `make fetch-data` populates.
#' @return The local file path, invisibly verified.
#' @export
use_dataset <- function(
    name,
    manifest = read_data_manifest(),
    raw_dir = here::here('analysis', 'data', 'raw_data')) {
  row <- manifest[manifest$name == name, , drop = FALSE]
  if (nrow(row) != 1L) {
    stop(sprintf("dataset '%s' must appear exactly once in the manifest",
                 name), call. = FALSE)
  }
  path <- file.path(raw_dir, row$container, row$object)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    stop(sprintf("dataset '%s' has no local copy at %s; run 'make %s'",
                 name, path, 'fetch-data'), call. = FALSE)
  }
  found <- digest::digest(file = path, algo = 'sha256')
  if (!identical(found, row$sha256)) {
    stop(sprintf(paste0("dataset '%s' does not match the manifest\n",
                        '  expected %s\n  found    %s\n',
                        "refusing to read it; re-run 'make fetch-data'"),
                 name, row$sha256, found), call. = FALSE)
  }
  entry <- data.frame(
    name    = name,
    remote  = row$remote,
    key     = paste(row$container, row$object, sep = '/'),
    sha256  = found,
    terms   = if ('terms' %in% names(row)) row$terms else NA_character_,
    read_at = format(Sys.time(), '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %Z')
  )
  prior <- .provenance$log
  if (!is.null(prior)) prior <- prior[prior$name != name, , drop = FALSE]
  .provenance$log <- rbind(prior, entry)
  path
}

#' Datasets read so far in this session
#'
#' @return A data frame with one row per dataset read through
#'   [use_dataset()], or a zero-row data frame if none were.
#' @export
data_provenance <- function() {
  if (is.null(.provenance$log)) {
    data.frame(name = character(), remote = character(),
               key = character(), sha256 = character(),
               terms = character(), read_at = character())
  } else {
    .provenance$log
  }
}

.git_lines <- function(args) {
  tryCatch(system2('git', args, stdout = TRUE, stderr = FALSE),
           error = function(e) NULL, warning = function(w) NULL)
}

#' The state of the code at this moment
#'
#' Uses the full commit hash rather than an abbreviated `git describe`,
#' and reports uncommitted changes to tracked files as a separate flag,
#' because a commit does not pin a working tree that differs from it.
#'
#' @return A list with `commit` (40 hex characters, or `NA` outside a
#'   repository) and `dirty` (`TRUE`, `FALSE`, or `NA`).
#' @export
code_state <- function() {
  commit <- .git_lines(c('rev-parse', 'HEAD'))
  if (is.null(commit) || !length(commit)) {
    return(list(commit = NA_character_, dirty = NA))
  }
  status <- .git_lines(c('status', '--porcelain', '--untracked-files=no'))
  list(commit = commit[[1]], dirty = length(status) > 0)
}

#' Write the session's data provenance beside a derived output
#'
#' Adds the code state so a derived file records both what it read and
#' exactly which commit read it.
#'
#' @param path Destination TSV.
#' @return `path`, invisibly.
#' @export
write_provenance <- function(path) {
  state <- code_state()
  prov <- data_provenance()
  prov$commit <- rep(state$commit, nrow(prov))
  prov$tree_dirty <- rep(state$dirty, nrow(prov))
  utils::write.table(prov, path, sep = '\t', quote = FALSE,
                     row.names = FALSE)
  invisible(path)
}

#' Register a rendered output's hash, code state, and inputs
#'
#' A document cannot contain its own hash, so the binding between a
#' rendered file and what produced it is written beside it, as one row
#' of a tab-separated register.
#'
#' @param output Path to the rendered file (PDF, HTML, or anything).
#' @param inputs A provenance data frame with `name` and `sha256`
#'   columns; defaults to the datasets read in this session.
#' @param register Path to the register TSV.
#' @return The appended row, invisibly.
#' @export
record_render <- function(
    output,
    inputs = data_provenance(),
    register = file.path(dirname(output), 'RENDERS.tsv')) {
  stopifnot(file.exists(output))
  state <- code_state()
  row <- data.frame(
    output        = basename(output),
    output_sha256 = digest::digest(file = output, algo = 'sha256'),
    commit        = state$commit,
    tree_dirty    = state$dirty,
    inputs        = paste(inputs$name, inputs$sha256, sep = '=',
                          collapse = ';'),
    recorded_at   = format(Sys.time(), '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %Z')
  )
  fresh <- !file.exists(register)
  utils::write.table(row, register, sep = '\t', quote = FALSE,
                     row.names = FALSE, col.names = fresh,
                     append = !fresh)
  invisible(row)
}

#' Look a rendered file up in the register by its hash
#'
#' The walk backward starts here: the bytes of the file in hand, not
#' its name, select the register row, which names the commit and the
#' input hashes.
#'
#' @param output Path to the rendered file being checked.
#' @param register Path to the register TSV.
#' @return The matching register row(s); errors if none match.
#' @export
verify_render <- function(
    output,
    register = file.path(dirname(output), 'RENDERS.tsv')) {
  reg <- utils::read.delim(register, colClasses = 'character')
  sha <- digest::digest(file = output, algo = 'sha256')
  hit <- reg[reg$output_sha256 == sha, , drop = FALSE]
  if (!nrow(hit)) {
    stop(sprintf(paste0("'%s' matches no registered render ",
                        '(sha256 %s); it was altered after rendering, ',
                        'or never registered'),
                 basename(output), substr(sha, 1, 12)), call. = FALSE)
  }
  hit
}

The two layers are independent, and the tests exercised both. With a tampered local copy, make analysis repaired the cache: the fetch step saw the mismatch, downloaded the object again, and the analysis ran on the right bytes. Running the script directly, with no fetch in front of it, stopped at the read (hashes abbreviated):

Error: dataset 'trial_extract_v3' does not match the manifest
  expected 77cad029cb5b0245c9df258f6898d3f9...
  found    b485c3f0a918e6175abbd21a1515d43a...
refusing to read it; re-run 'make fetch-data'

Move 4: ignore the bytes

# .gitignore
analysis/data/raw_data/

The repository carries the manifest and never the data. A fresh clone plus make fetch-data reconstitutes the project, and deleting raw_data/ to reclaim disk is safe.

What this buys

No machine is authoritative and nothing needs reconciling. Two people working from the same manifest work from bit-identical inputs, and their provenance files prove it. The question behind the whole reproducibility apparatus, which data produced Table 1, has an answer recoverable from the commit and checkable against the bytes.

How it was tested

Both test scripts copy the example to a temporary directory, so running them never modifies it. tests/run-local.sh uses an rclone alias remote pointing at a local directory. tests/run-s3.sh starts SeaweedFS 4.47 on the loopback interface with per-run credentials for a publisher and a read-only identity, and a bucket under object lock in COMPLIANCE mode with a one-day retention. Both ran on 2026-09-28 on macOS arm64.
